title: LINQ set ops & list reconciliation
description: Reconciling a stored collection with an incoming payload — the PUT-a-collection interview question: Except / Intersect / DistinctBy / ExceptBy-style keyed diffs, membership through ToHashSet, MinBy/MaxBy, Zip, and the vacuous truths of Any/All on empty input. Nearest existing units: csbootcamp 03 (the LINQ core verbs) and jstrain-cs 04/02-05 and 03/02-03 (HashSet set algebra) — here the operators are applied to reconciliation problems, never re-toured.

exercises.title: Sync a tag list: added and removed
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The client sends the complete list of tag ids for a post. How do you turn that PUT into the inserts and deletes the database needs?"

**Contract.** `Added` is every id the incoming list has that the stored list lacks; `Removed` is every id the stored list has that the incoming list lacks. `Except` is a SET operation: its result is distinct, so a payload that repeats an id produces it once — exactly what you want when the ids become INSERT rows.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `List<int> Added(List<int> current, List<int> incoming)` → the distinct ids the payload has and the store lacks
- `List<int> Removed(List<int> current, List<int> incoming)` → the distinct ids the store has and the payload lacks

**Worked example.** Stored `[1, 2, 3]`, incoming `[2, 3, 4]` → added **[4]**, removed **[1]**; 2 and 3 are untouched.
exercises.explanation:
`Except` walks its receiver and keeps each distinct element the argument does not contain, so the direction of the call decides the question.

For stored `[1, 2, 3]` and incoming `[2, 3, 4]`:
- `incoming.Except(current)` → 4 is the only incoming id missing from the store → **[4]** (insert)
- `current.Except(incoming)` → 1 is the only stored id missing from the payload → **[1]** (delete)

Diffing a full-collection PUT into two small sets is what keeps the write proportional to the change instead of "delete everything, reinsert everything".
hints: A full-list PUT is two questions — what is new, and what disappeared — and one set operator answers both if you call it in both directions.
a.Except(b) yields the distinct elements of a that are not in b; added = incoming minus current, removed = current minus incoming.
Except keeps the distinct members of its receiver that the argument lacks — run it both directions, incoming against current for additions and current against incoming for removals

exercises.title: Kept items and "did anything change?"
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The PUT body might be identical to what is stored — how do you detect a no-op, and does reordering the list count as a change?"

**Contract.** `Kept` is the members present in both lists, in the incoming list's order. `SameList` is strict: same members, same order, same length. `SameItemsAnyOrder` is set equality: neither list has a member the other lacks — order is ignored and so are duplicates (`["a"]` and `["a", "a"]` count as the same set; that caveat is the thing to say out loud in an interview).

**Your task.** Implement the three stubbed local functions:
- `List<string> Kept(List<string> current, List<string> incoming)` → the members present in both lists, in the incoming order
- `bool SameList(List<string> a, List<string> b)` → true only for the same members in the same order
- `bool SameItemsAnyOrder(List<string> a, List<string> b)` → true when neither list has a member the other lacks

**Worked example.** `["a", "b"]` vs `["b", "a"]`: `SameList` → **false**, `SameItemsAnyOrder` → **true**.
exercises.explanation:
Three different notions of "the same", each one line of LINQ.

For `a = ["a", "b"]`, `b = ["b", "a"]`:
- `SequenceEqual` compares position by position: "a" vs "b" differs at index 0 → **false**
- `a.Except(b)` is empty and `b.Except(a)` is empty → **true** for the any-order check

Outside a LINQ drill the any-order check is usually `a.ToHashSet().SetEquals(b)`: one hash set, one pass over `b`, and it reads as exactly the question being asked.

Pick the notion your domain means: a ranked list changes when it is reordered, a tag set does not — and set equality silently treats duplicates as one.
hints: Ask first whether order is part of the data: a ranking cares, a set of tags does not.
Intersect keeps the receiver's order; SequenceEqual is element-by-element; two sets are equal when each Except the other is empty.
Intersect keeps the receiver's order, SequenceEqual demands identical order, and mutual emptiness of Except in both directions means the same member set regardless of order or duplicates

exercises.title: Dedupe signups by canonical email
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Your CSV import has `Ann@Example.com` and `ann@example.com` — the same person twice. Deduplicate without losing the order of the file."

**Contract.** Two emails are the same person when their lowercase-invariant forms are equal. The FIRST spelling encountered is the one kept, and the surviving entries stay in input order. The output keeps the original spelling (you are deduplicating, not normalizing the data).

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `List<string> DedupeEmails(List<string> emails)` → `DistinctBy` on `e.ToLowerInvariant()`, as a list

**Worked example.** `["A@x.com", "a@x.com", "b@x.com"]` → **["A@x.com", "b@x.com"]** — "a@x.com" collapses into the earlier "A@x.com".
exercises.explanation:
`DistinctBy` remembers each projected key it has seen and yields an element only the first time its key appears.

For `["A@x.com", "a@x.com", "b@x.com"]`:
- "A@x.com" → key "a@x.com", new → kept
- "a@x.com" → key "a@x.com", already seen → dropped
- "b@x.com" → key "b@x.com", new → kept → **["A@x.com", "b@x.com"]**

Deduplicate on a canonical KEY while keeping the original value: the projection decides identity, the element you keep is untouched.
hints: Identity is not the raw string here — decide what canonical form makes two emails "the same", and compare on that.
DistinctBy(keySelector) keeps the first element for each distinct key; ToLowerInvariant gives a culture-proof key.
DistinctBy keeps the first element for each projected key, so project every email to its lowercase-invariant form and let the operator keep the earliest spelling

exercises.title: Validate a batch of ids in one pass
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A bulk-delete request names 500 ids. Before touching anything, report which of them do not exist — without 500 scans of the table snapshot."

**Contract.** Both answers are over the DISTINCT requested ids, in the order each id first appears in the request. `MissingIds` keeps the ones absent from `existing`; `KnownIds` keeps the ones present. Membership must be a hash lookup: materialize `existing` into a set once, then probe it.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `List<int> MissingIds(List<int> requested, List<int> existing)` → distinct requested ids not in `existing.ToHashSet()`
- `List<int> KnownIds(List<int> requested, List<int> existing)` → distinct requested ids that are in it

**Worked example.** Requested `[5, 6, 7]`, existing `[6]` → missing **[5, 7]**.
exercises.explanation:
`existing.ToHashSet()` pays O(m) once; every probe afterwards is O(1), so the whole check is O(n + m) instead of O(n·m).

For requested `[5, 6, 7]` against existing `[6]`:
- set = {6}
- 5 → not in set → missing; 6 → in set → known; 7 → not in set → missing → **[5, 7]**

`List.Contains` inside a loop is the quiet quadratic of batch endpoints — one `ToHashSet` removes it.
hints: Calling Contains on a List inside a loop is a linear scan per id — what structure makes each membership test constant time?
existing.ToHashSet() once, then requested.Distinct() filtered by set.Contains (or its negation).
Materialize the existing ids into a hash set once, then walk the distinct requested ids and partition them by set membership, keeping first-seen order

exercises.title: Cheapest plan and price spread
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Given the plans, return the NAME of the cheapest one, and the gap between the cheapest and the dearest."

**Contract.** `MinBy` returns the whole ELEMENT with the smallest projected key (not the key itself), and on a tie it returns the FIRST such element in sequence order. The spread is the projected maximum minus the projected minimum; a single plan has spread 0. Inputs are never empty.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `string CheapestName(List<(string Name, int Cents)> items)` → the name of the plan with the lowest price, the first one on a tie
- `int PriceSpread(List<(string Name, int Cents)> items)` → the highest price minus the lowest price

**Worked example.** `[("a", 300), ("b", 150), ("c", 900)]` → cheapest **"b"**, spread 900 − 150 = **750**.
exercises.explanation:
`Min(i => i.Cents)` would hand back 150 and lose which plan it was; `MinBy(i => i.Cents)` hands back the tuple `("b", 150)` itself.

For `[("a", 300), ("b", 150), ("c", 900)]`:
- `MinBy` → ("b", 150) → name **"b"**
- spread = `Max` 900 − `Min` 150 = **750**

Reach for `MinBy`/`MaxBy` whenever you need the element that wins, not the winning number — and remember ties go to the earliest element.
hints: Min gives you the smallest number; you need the item that owns it.
MinBy(keySelector) returns the element with the least key, first one on ties; the spread is Max(key) − Min(key).
MinBy hands back the whole element whose projected key is smallest, first one on a tie — the spread subtracts the projected minimum from the projected maximum

exercises.title: Zip two parallel columns into labels
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Two columns of a CSV were parsed into separate lists. Combine them into display labels — and what does your code do if one column is shorter?"

**Contract.** `Labels` pairs element i of `names` with element i of `qty` and formats `"{name} x{qty}"`. `Zip` stops at the SHORTER sequence without any error — extra elements are silently dropped. `PairedCount` reports how many pairs that is, so a caller can compare it with both lengths and decide whether truncation is acceptable.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `List<string> Labels(List<string> names, List<int> qty)` → element `i` of each list formatted `"{name} x{qty}"`, for as many positions as BOTH lists have
- `int PairedCount(List<string> names, List<int> qty)` → how many such pairs there are

**Worked example.** `["pen", "cup"]` with `[2, 3]` → **["pen x2", "cup x3"]**.
exercises.explanation:
`Zip` advances both enumerators together and ends the moment either one is exhausted.

For `["pen"]` with `[2, 3]`:
- step 1: "pen" + 2 → "pen x2"
- step 2: names is exhausted → stop; the 3 is dropped → **["pen x2"]**

Silent truncation is a data-loss bug waiting to happen at an import boundary: count the pairs and compare with both inputs when a mismatch should be an error.
hints: Pairing element i with element i is a built-in operator — what does it do when one list runs out first?
Zip(second, resultSelector) stops at the shorter sequence; the pair count is the minimum of the two counts.
Zip walks both sequences in lockstep and quietly stops at the shorter one, so the paired count is the smaller of the two lengths — decide on purpose whether silent truncation is acceptable

exercises.title: Any/All on empty collections
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "`if (invoices.All(i => i.Paid)) UnlockPremium();` — what happens for a customer with no invoices yet?"

**Contract.** `AnyOverdue` is true when at least one entry is greater than 0. `AllPaid` is true when every balance equals 0. Implement them with `Any` and `All` exactly — and notice the empty-input answers: `Any` over nothing is **false**, `All` over nothing is **true** (vacuous truth: there is no counter-example). The tests pin both, so that you see the behavior a guard clause inherits.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions with `Any` and `All`:
- `bool AnyOverdue(List<int> daysLate)` → true when at least one entry is above 0
- `bool AllPaid(List<int> balancesCents)` → true when every balance is 0

**Worked example.** `AllPaid([])` → **true** — a customer with no invoices passes an all-paid check.
exercises.explanation:
`All` returns false as soon as it finds an element failing the predicate; with no elements it never finds one, so it returns true.

For `AllPaid([])`:
- no elements → no counter-example → **true**
- `AnyOverdue([])` mirrors it: no element satisfies the predicate → **false**

When "no items" must not count as success, guard it explicitly (`list.Count > 0 && list.All(...)`) — the operator will not do it for you.
hints: Think about what each operator does when there is nothing to look at.
Any(pred) needs one witness (empty → false); All(pred) needs zero counter-examples (empty → true).
Any over an empty sequence is false and All over an empty sequence is true by vacuous truth — guard the empty case separately when 'no items' must not count as success

exercises.title: Client cache sync by id and version
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The client has `(Id, Version)` for each cached record. Given the server's list, which records must the client re-download, and which has it never seen?"

**Contract.** Compare per ID, not per pair. An id needs a **refresh** when the client has it AND the server holds it at a strictly higher version (equal versions are up to date). An id is **new** when the server has it and no client entry carries that id. Ids the client has but the server lacks are out of scope here (that is the delete question). Both results follow the server list's order. Do it in O(n + m): build ONE lookup of the client's versions keyed by id, then walk the server list once. A `client.Any(...)` inside a loop over the server list is the same quiet quadratic that drill 04 removes. (Client ids are unique.)

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `List<int> ToRefresh(List<(int Id, int Ver)> client, List<(int Id, int Ver)> server)` → the server ids the client holds at a strictly LOWER version
- `List<int> NewOnServer(List<(int Id, int Ver)> client, List<(int Id, int Ver)> server)` → the server ids no client entry carries

**Worked example.** Client `(1,1) (2,3) (3,2)`, server `(1,2) (2,3) (4,1)` → refresh **[1]**, new **[4]**.
exercises.explanation:
Pair-level set operators get this wrong: `(1,1)` and `(1,2)` are different tuples, so a naive `server.Except(client)` would call id 1 "new". Project to ids and compare versions per id.

For client `(1,1) (2,3) (3,2)` and server `(1,2) (2,3) (4,1)`:
- id 1: client v1 < server v2 → refresh
- id 2: v3 = v3 → up to date
- id 4: no client entry with id 4 → new
- → refresh **[1]**, new **[4]**

`ExceptBy(client ids, s => s.Id)` is the keyed form of `Except`: it compares the PROJECTED key but hands back whole server entries, so the set difference and the projection are one operator. A `Dictionary<int, int>` of client versions makes the refresh check one lookup per server entry instead of a scan of the client list.

Choose the key before choosing the operator: identity is the id, freshness is the version.
hints: Two tuples with the same id but different versions are different values — decide what identifies a record before you diff.
Refresh: client.ToDictionary(c => c.Id, c => c.Ver), then keep server entries whose id is found at a lower version. New: server.ExceptBy(client ids, s => s.Id).
An entry needs a refresh when the server holds the same id at a strictly higher version, and it is new when its id appears in no client entry — project ids and compare per id, not per pair
